description: We're excited to be building a SphereX web tool!
summary: Wink is a sky exploration tool, using near-infrared images over various bands from SPHEREx to map out astronomical phenomena and their changes over time. Users can input any position, and Wink will not only fetch multiple frames to click through, but also use its (in-development) AI model to predict what is likely moving and what is changing in brightness. Importantly, users can also be citizen scientists and help find potential movers, contributing to a community of amateur astronomers. Wink also includes a gallery of pre-determined targets and plots these targets on its Sky Dome, a 360-degree view of the night sky. Perhaps the most important part for the general applicability of our project, we include learning resources on our education page to make this project accessible even for people with no background in physics or math (our minimum requirement is knowing multiplication).
details:
What exactly does Wink do?

Wink is a sky exploration tool, using near-infrared images over various bands from SPHEREx to map out astronomical phenomena and their changes over time. Users can input any position, and Wink will fetch multiple frames to blink through, and users should be able to detect changes from the blinks. Wink also includes a gallery of pre-determined targets and plots these targets on its Sky Dome, a 360-degree grid view of the night sky. 

We have implemented an education page for users who may be new to astronomy and the SPHEREx mission, giving them lessons on infrared light, the coordinate system, and a basic overview of the SPHEREx mission. We want to get users to know the concepts behind Wink, enabling everyone from students and amateurs to professionals to understand and use our many tools. The page opens with an interactive lesson to get the user familiar with our tool. We have them try to spot a mover on an example image, then on another image, and have them change between the different bands to see the object. We then show the blink feature and what could be inferred. On the next page, we show the user how SHPEREx could find Planet X, and lastly we show how we know an object actually moved rather than it being its natural shift, having the user interact with a graph on a star's natural drift. For the rest of the education page, we include things such as an overview on how Right Ascension (RA) and Declination (Dec) work and why some stars move for a basic introduction to astronomy concepts. It then gives an introduction to the SPHEREx mission, giving an overview of the 102 bands of infrared light it uses and also where users can find the public data. We then cover the history of Planet X, where the idea came from and that the users don’t need to be professionals and that amateurs have found many different objects and its tools like Wink that can allow anyone to delve into the world of astronomy to learn and potentially discover new things. 

To search for the objects SPHEREx has found, Wink offers many ways to do so. First is through our raw search which the user manually types in the Right Ascension and Declination which would then attempt to load the image for that part of the sky. This process of loading up the image from the server can take two to four minutes to clean and process the images. Our second option is the look through our gallery which offers 100 pre-loaded and pre-determined targets for quick access to our users; with just one, you can look at how the object moves with every blink. Our last option for searching is using our filtered search which allows our users to sift through different objects such as brown dwarfs or even regions in the sky to allow the users to look for more specific results. 

Through whatever medium the user selects to search for their object, they will all be eventually redirected to the same page: the viewer page. Here, you can press play through the SPHEREx image or manually click through the frames. There are different ways we offer to view the image: you can view the image at separate dates, which is the default option; you can view with all the dates in one, which can better show which objects move the most; and a subtracted image, which, when you click play, shows the objects that actually moved. On the right sidebar, you can check and uncheck the different layers and also overlay known stars from the Gaia, WISE, and 2MASS catalogues. Underneath that, we have the settings for brightness and exposure, which can be adjusted with the sidebar. You are also allowed to invert the colors of the image and use the crosshair. We have attempted to implement an AI model that predicts the movers in the image and how much they move with the blinks. You can also change which band of wavelength you want to view the image in, with six different ranges of wavelength and the default option, which is all 102 bands. When a user finds a mover, they can mark it by clicking “Mark this” under report a find, and if it ends up actually being a mover, it will be marked on the community finds where everyone is able to see each other's findings. 

One additional feature we have for visualizing the objects in the sky is our Sky Dome. We wanted to give our users a more interactive place where they can easily visualize where objects are in space, as if they were looking into a telescope of the entire night sky. The Sky Dome provides a 360-degree view of the sky with marked locations of our 100 pre-loaded objects. The dome is loaded in with a grid to better help users understand where they are exactly looking at in space. When you click on one of these pre-loaded objects you are given quick info about the object and get a look at what band you are looking at. You can sweep through both the band and the dates for the image just like on the viewer page. You also have the option to be redirected to the viewer page for a more detailed view of the image. 

Of course, this is still a work in progress, so there are certain features of the project that are not entirely developed. One of these is our AI mover detection program, which is currently in a prototyping/developmental phase and requires significantly more data and testing to refine and turn into something reliable. Also included in this is our idea for a filtered search, which currently doesn’t have any asteroid or comet movers due to their fast speeds making it hard to capture them across one small field of view. We’d also like to find ways to make our public-facing abilities (like marking) more easily accessible for users. Some of our features are technically made but not fully implemented, such as a simulator that lets you add fake marks to real images to visualize how even a real object may not be completely or easily picked up by a detector (this fits into our broader goal of education so that amateurs can understand how the focus of SPHEREx is more on coverage than specific accuracy.

How does Wink work?

We take data from the SphereX mission from IRSA, then we find groups that are 6 months apart with the assistance of Gaia/CatWISE.

Instead of downloading huge chunks of data at a time, which would be incredibly difficult to do especially during a time like the hackathon when the servers are having many requests sent to them, we just read a small field-of-view square to get all the images associated with our target.

Cleaning is one of the most important parts of how the data is processed once it’s in our hands. Because the SPHEREx images are handed to us with certain attributes for each pixel, we go pixel-by-pixel and more accurately tune to what an actual look at the sky might look like by accounting for what the telescope tells us about its data collection. This includes subtracting zodiacal light, masking over pixels that have experienced a flag that turns them into a bad pixel (could be caused by detector, cosmic rays, satellite trails, noise, etc.)

To improve the signal-to-noise ratio (to make sure we’re giving as accurate a photo as possible, because even though some photos may cross our 5σ baseline requirement it’s still better to have better data), we combine several of the detector’s layers together into one image and stack them. In fact, we even make a special consideration for brown dwarfs, creating a cold stack specifically for them (that utilizes the colder wavelengths, aka detectors 5 and 6).

Before sending any of this data off, we try to look for movers via change in position or brightness across dates. If we find potential candidates, they’re checked against Gaia, CatWISE and 2MASS to see for existence.

Finally, we arrange the files for export as PNG frames, then pack them into a JSON. We also make the necessary SkyDome tiles. Finally, we add them to the gallery if they belong there.

Why Wink?

The main benefit we see from this web page is it allows anybody of any skill level to learn more about the SPHEREx mission and what it has found. Our primary goal here is to make the results of NASA’s SPHEREx available to all of the general public, because NASA is something that the entire American public helps fund and support, and that can only come by making sure the details of the project are understandable even for someone without a major background in physics or astronomy.

Wink offers a way for amateurs and professionals to interact with each other. We hope to see people using this tool both to make discoveries as citizen scientists and also to enhance their own understanding of common practices in astronomy. For both the expert and the amateur, our product aims to provide a holistic and powerful view into the universe around us in 102 bands of infrared!

What tools did we use for Wink?

We used Vercel and Render to host our site and load our images. We utilized Supabase for saving the marks the users make on the images so it can be seen across different devices and networks. All our code lives in a GitHub repo. For our data, we used the SPHEREx data given to us, Gaia DR3, and CatWISE2020 catalogues given to us via the resource tab on the Space Apps Challenge page. All the data processing code is in Python, with the front end being done in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. For our use of Super Intelligence (SI), our first initial use of it was to learn about astrophysics, data processing, data visualization, and UI/UX, all of which we envisioned to be key focuses of the project. We made detailed learning modules so that we could split ourselves up into being the main expert on one of these roles and a backup on the other, and then we combined that knowledge together to build our product. Beyond that, we used Claude for parts of the data fetching, coding, and building it in as our AI/SI prototype. We made it an explicit focus of our project to ensure SI was not used in any creative application. Hence, the UI/UX, although coded by Claude, are based entirely on hand-drawn drawings of the website. Similarly, all storytelling elements (including this description) are written by us, as we feel that SI would not accurately capture the motivations and emotions behind our project and its goals.
